title: Κύκνος ⟨ἀντὶ χηνὸς ἀπαχθείς⟩
titleEn: The Swan Taken Instead of the Goose
part: The Swan Taken Instead of the Goose (Chambry 173)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 173. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀνὴρ εὐπορῶν χῆνά τε ἅμα καὶ κύκνον ἔτρεφεν, οὐκ ἐπὶ τοῖς αὐτοῖς μέντοι· τὸν μὲν γὰρ ᾠδῆς, τὸν δὲ τραπέζης ἕνεκεν.
sentences.tr: Anēr euporōn chēna te hama kai kyknon etrephen, ouk epi tois autois mentoi· ton men gar ōidēs, ton de trapezēs heneken.
sentences.l: A man being well off kept a goose and at the same time a swan, not for the same ends however; the one for the sake of song, the other for the sake of the table.
sentences.n: εὐπορῶν is a participle of εὐπορέω, to be well provided, and stands where English would say "a man of means". ἕνεκεν comes after its noun and governs both genitives at once, ᾠδῆς and τραπέζης. The μέν clause takes up the swan and the δέ clause the goose, so the pair is picked up in the reverse of the order in which it was named — it is the swan that sings.

sentences.t: Ἐπεὶ δὲ ἔδει τὸν χῆνα παθεῖν ἐφ’ οἷς ἐτρέφετο, νὺξ μὲν ἦν, καὶ διαγινώσκειν ὁ καιρὸς οὐκ ἀφῆκεν ἑκάτερον.
sentences.tr: Epei de edei ton chēna pathein eph’ hois etrepheto, nyx men ēn, kai diaginōskein ho kairos ouk aphēken hekateron.
sentences.l: But when the goose had to undergo the thing for which he was being kept, it was night, and the hour did not allow one to tell the two apart.
sentences.i: But when the time came for the goose to undergo what he had been kept for, it was night, and the hour left no way of telling the two birds apart.
sentences.n: ἔδει is impersonal, "it was necessary", with the accusative τὸν χῆνα and the infinitive παθεῖν. ἐφ’ οἷς stands for ἐπὶ τούτοις ἐφ’ οἷς, "on the terms on which": the antecedent is left out and the one preposition serves both, so the dative is ἐπί's own and not an attraction. ἀφίημι with an infinitive is to let a thing go forward, to permit it; ἑκάτερον, "each of the two", is the object of διαγινώσκειν.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ κύκνος, ἀντὶ τοῦ χηνὸς ἀπαχθείς, ᾄδει τι μέλος θανάτου προοίμιον, καὶ τῇ μὲν ᾠδῇ μηνύει τὴν φύσιν, τὴν δὲ τελευτὴν διαφεύγει τῷ μέλει.
sentences.tr: Ho de kyknos, anti tou chēnos apachtheis, āidei ti melos thanatou prooimion, kai tēi men ōidēi mēnyei tēn physin, tēn de teleutēn diapheugei tōi melei.
sentences.l: But the swan, led off instead of the goose, sings a strain, a prelude of death, and by the song he makes his nature known, but his end he escapes by the melody.
sentences.i: But the swan, taken off in the goose's place, sings a strain that is death's prelude; by the singing he betrays what he is, and by the music escapes his end.
sentences.n: ᾄδει is a historic present, dropping into the present tense at the turn of the story. προοίμιον stands in apposition to μέλος: the song is itself the opening prelude to his death. μέν … δέ sets the two effects of one song against each other. The Greeks held that swans sing only as they die, so the singing is at once the sign of the swan's kind and the thing that saves him.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι πολλάκις ἡ μουσικὴ τελευτῆς ἀναβολὴν ἀπεργάζεται.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti pollakis hē mousikē teleutēs anabolēn apergazetai.
sentences.l: The fable shows that often music brings about a postponement of death.
sentences.n: ἀναβολή is a putting off, a delay, with τελευτῆς the genitive of what is deferred; ἀπεργάζομαι is to work a thing out to completion. μουσική is wider than "music" — the whole art of the Muses — but here it is the singing itself.
